what: The URL Encoder / Decoder makes text safe to use inside a web address, and turns encoded addresses full of % signs back into readable text. This is also called percent-encoding. For example, a space becomes %20 and an ampersand becomes %26.

It helps web developers, marketers who build tracking links, SEO workers and anyone who copies links with strange codes in them. Use it when you put a search term or name into a link, or when you want to read what an encoded link really says.
Encoding and decoding run in your browser, and nothing you paste is sent anywhere.
uses: Put a value into a link
Encode a search term, a name or an email address before you add it after ? or & in a URL.
Decode a link from an email or a log file so you can see the real words and parameters.
Encode campaign names that contain spaces or symbols so analytics tools read them correctly.
Encode a full link with the structure option ticked so spaces and non-English letters become valid, but the slashes and ? stay as they are.
Decode form or query data where + stands for a space to see what a user really typed.
tutorial: Click in the “Text or URL” box and paste a single value, such as a search term, or a complete link.
Below the buttons is the checkbox “Keep URL structure (do not encode : / ? & = #)”. Tick it when you work with a whole link. Leave it unticked for a single value that goes inside a link.
Click “Encode”. The text in the box is replaced with the encoded version and the message says “Encoded.”.
Click “Decode” to turn % codes back into normal characters. With the checkbox unticked, every + is also turned into a space, as in form data. With it ticked, + is kept as it is.
Click “Copy” to copy the whole box to your clipboard and paste it into your link or code.
Click “Clear” to empty the box and the message.
features: Unticked encodes every special character, which is right for one value. Ticked keeps : / ? & = # so a full link still works.
When decoding a single value, + is treated as a space, the way HTML forms send data.
Non-English letters and emoji are encoded as UTF-8 % codes and decoded back correctly.
A broken % code gives a plain message instead of a wrong result.
Same box for input and output
You can encode, check and decode again without copying text between boxes.
One click copies the result or empties the box.

example.title: Worked example: encoding a search term and a full link
example.text: Leave the checkbox unticked, type coffee & cake: 50% off and click “Encode”. The box shows coffee%20%26%20cake%3A%2050%25%20off. Each space became %20, & became %26, the colon became %3A and % became %25. Now click “Clear”, tick “Keep URL structure”, paste https://example.com/search?q=coffee & cake and click “Encode”. The result is https://example.com/search?q=coffee%20&%20cake, so only the spaces changed. Without the tick, the same link becomes https%3A%2F%2Fexample.com%2Fsearch%3Fq%3Dcoffee%20%26%20cake, which no longer works as a link.

tips: Encode each value on its own, with the box unticked, before you join values into a link. This is the safest way.
If a value contains & or =, it must be encoded unticked. Otherwise the & starts a new parameter and breaks your link.
When decoding a full link that may contain a real + sign, tick the checkbox so the + is not turned into a space.
If a link shows %2520, it was encoded twice. Click “Decode” twice to get the original text.
Spaces are encoded as %20, not +. Both are read as a space in most query strings.
problems: “This text contains a broken % sequence and cannot be decoded.”
There is a % that is not followed by two hexadecimal digits, for example 50% off. Encode the text first, or fix the % codes by hand.
My full link stopped working after encoding
The checkbox was unticked, so the : and / characters were encoded too. Click “Decode”, tick “Keep URL structure”, and click “Encode” again.
A + sign turned into a space
With the checkbox unticked, “Decode” treats + as a space. Tick the checkbox before decoding if the + is real.
Some % codes stay after decoding with the box ticked
In structure mode, codes for characters like / ? & = # are kept encoded on purpose. Untick the checkbox and decode again to turn them back.
